#35787. Change these settings if you want GTA 6 to feel like old GTA

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (988 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Change these settings if you want GTA 6 to feel like old GTA

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto 6 has many new features and updates that bring the series up to date, from the intertwined Wanted and Heat systems that keep cops on the hunt for the protagonists even after they respray their car, to charging infrastructure for electric vehicles.
  • Once GTA 6 eventually comes to PC (which could be as soon as early 2027), it's all but certain that a swathe of mods will emerge to restore gameplay elements from previous titles.
  • One of the ways in which Rockstar brought GTA 6 into the modern age is by making a key change to the control system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are few ways you can wind back the clock.

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto 6 has many new features and updates that bring the series up to date, from the intertwined Wanted and Heat systems that keep cops on the hunt for the protagonists even after they respray their car, to charging infrastructure for electric vehicles. Still, some players might be missing certain aspects of previous titles in the series that developer Rockstar Games has either moved on from or no longer made the default option.

Once GTA 6 eventually comes to PC (which could be as soon as early 2027), it's all but certain that a swathe of mods will emerge to restore gameplay elements from previous titles. However, you don't need to wait until then to wind back the clock, at least to a certain extent. There are some in-game settings you can change to restore more of a classic GTA feel, but that might come at the expense of more convenient quality-of-life improvements.

One of the ways in which Rockstar brought GTA 6 into the modern age is by making a key change to the control system. For many years, GTA players may have had to give their thumb a bit of a workout when they wanted to sprint. By default, the console versions of GTA 5 require players to mash the X button on PlayStation or A on Xbox to help them high-tail it to their destination. The settings allow you to change this so you can hold down the button instead, which is an improvement.

However, many found it inconvenient to have this core movement function mapped to a face button instead of a thumbstick. Lots of other game developers have long assigned the sprint function to the left thumbstick, so you just need to click the same thing you're using to move your character to make them speed up.

According to recent reports, rockstar finally got with the program in GTA 6 by assigning the run button to L3 on PS5 and LS on Xbox by default. But maybe you really hate your thumb or for some reason just really liked how the sprint function worked in the previous games.

To return to the old movement control system, hit the pause button and go to the settings. On the control scheme page, you can change the setup from Default to Classic. This assigns run/sprint to X on a PS5 controller and A on Xbox, with the crouch ability moved to L3/LS instead, and jump to Square (PS5) or X (Xbox). In an ideal world, GTA 6 would have fully remappable controls so you could set up the control system however you want. But if you really want that classic GTA feel, you can at least make this change.

Sources indicate that one of the main drawbacks of GTA 6 for me after playing the game for 12 hours is that Rockstar hasn't upgraded its shooting mechanics well enough. It's tough to aim accurately — just ask the NPC whose hand I accidentally hit while we were horsing around and doing a whole William Tell thing. The inevitable PC version of the game will at least let players use their mouse for aiming. However, there are aim assist options that can help in the meantime.

For one thing, you can use a similar targeting option to the one found in GTA 5. In the gameplay tab of the GTA 6 settings, scroll down to the combat section and change the Targeting option from Partial to Lock-On. According to the description, this means the game will try to automatically lock onto the closest target when you're aiming. If you enable the Lock-On Target Switch option, you'll be able to flick between nearby targets using the right thumbstick.

This section of the settings menu also allows you to adjust the aim assist strength to your liking. There's also a Shooting Assist option (which helps with tracking targets that are close by) and a way to enable auto-aiming for drive-by shootings. That noted, if you're a crackshot with a controller and confident in your accuracy, you can go in the other direction and select the free aim Targeting option.

Industry observers note that GTA old heads who have been with the series since the very beginning (hi!) may remember that, in the earliest games, there was no built-in navigation help other than directional arrows that only showed you where to go as the crow flies. You had to navigate the road network all by yourself, relying on your memory, perhaps a printed map and maybe some notes to help you get around. Even getting to the location where you could save your progress in GTA 2 was a pain.

Since then, we've all grown used to minimaps and compasses that help us get to where we want to go. Those are often very useful in open-world games, which have grown in vastly in scope over the last three decades.

But if you really want a challenge in GTA 6 — and a taste of what things were like in the original 1997 game — you can minimize the navigation help in the latest title. In the UI section of the settings menu, you can switch off the minimap, compass, GPS routes and in-world objective markers and largely rely on your wits.

I recommend that you don't disable all of these features, to be clear. The world of GTA 6 is vast and dense. Getting around and knowing where to go without using any of these tools would be very difficult. But, if you want a true old-school GTA feel or want to make the game as immersive as possible, tinkering with the navigation systems is something you can try. Unlike in GTA 2, though, at least you won't have to zip over to the local church to save your progress.

As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a upcoming threat is rising: the teals

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns.

  • The Fresh South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

The Fresh South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.

This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

In a recent development, this weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.

Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.

In a recent development, “Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she remarked. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”.

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.

Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

In a recent development, the independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, revealed last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.

Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.

Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

In a recent development, at the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.

The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.

“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.

This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.

During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.

Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.

But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

Sources indicate that in the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.

If all independents were successful – and that is a massive if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.

Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

According to recent reports, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CEO Elon Musk stated SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.

These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk remarked, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

“We’ve got a plan that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the organization is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

Industry observers note that combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he stated. According to Musk, the manufacturer has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”.

Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”.

The idea isn’t upcoming, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said during the company’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use massive cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.

In a recent development, even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk mentioned one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

SpaceX’s plan to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he noted, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”.

Breaking: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army confirmed Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air.
  • Industry observers note that the Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs).
  • It has been revealed that “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army confirmed Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

Industry observers note that the Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

It has been revealed that “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”.

It has been revealed that telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

Lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army noted. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”.

According to recent reports, in an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army remarked that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”.

The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it remarked the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

In a recent development, in all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” plan the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army stated the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”.

According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the initiative is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

According to recent reports, the Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

In a recent development, modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

According to recent reports, during the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

The Army’s plan was to communicate clearly with the public about the looks, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

According to recent reports, in its environmental risk assessment, the Army stated it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”.

Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the strategy.

“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

On Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the strategy “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting prepares until it can review the case.

Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:.

The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”.

This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.

Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person noted, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical fresh insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have remarked.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it notes is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the upcoming intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Sources indicate that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, stated at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

According to recent reports, still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Signal now blocks screenshots by default to stymie AI agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (470 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The company is calling for a simple way for developers to opt out of AI snooping.
  • Signal views AI agents built into phones as an "existential threat," and it's acting accordingly.
  • Industry observers note that the measures keep Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence from snooping on your chats, at least to a degree.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The company is calling for a simple way for developers to opt out of AI snooping.

Signal views AI agents built into phones as an "existential threat," and it's acting accordingly. The encrypted messaging app said Friday that it will block screenshots by default on iOS 27, and on Android when AI assistants try to capture the screen.

Industry observers note that the measures keep Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence from snooping on your chats, at least to a degree. The assistants are designed to help people by reading what's on the screen and pulling in information to better answer their questions. But the byproduct is that chats meant to be private — including encrypted ones — can end up on a remote server outside your or Signal's control.

The move echoes one from last year, when Signal blocked Microsoft's Recall from snapshotting chats on Windows 11.

Signal's concerns aren't limited to the built-in assistants. It's also worried about third-party agents like Meta's Muse, which Reuters caught reading Signal messages via permissions granted during setup. On Android, it read messages from notifications; on Mac, it used accessibility permissions, which Signal warns can be exploited "as a skeleton key.".

The new settings are slightly different on iOS and Android. On iPhone, a new "Block Siri AI" setting is on by default. On Android, Signal uses its existing "Screen security" option. On both platforms, you'll see a prompt offering to turn the protection off when it detects either a screenshot (iOS) or an AI assistant reading the screen (Android).

But that protection only goes so far. If the other person has switched protections off, blocking screenshots on your end won't stop an AI assistant or agent from reading your messages on the other person's device. It also won't prevent third-party agents from reading notifications or digging through files. Signal says operating system makers don't offer a way for developers to restrict AI access "without making drastic compromises to the core user experience." On Mac, that leaves Signal without any user protections at all.

Recent findings suggest that in some ways, this mirrors the problem with AI glasses, which can record bystanders without their knowledge or consent. That's led to them being banned in some public places, like courtrooms and schools, and being shunned as "perv glasses." Privacy in the age of AI is becoming less of an individual setting and more of a communal choice, with laws and social shaming being some of the only recourse individuals have.

Recent findings suggest that as for Signal, it wants a standard, system-level way to block AI agents from reading apps' content. It says it's talking with Apple and Google and is cautiously optimistic about where that's headed. Until then, know that "privacy" is a relative term at best.

Latest Update: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.
  • That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.
  • Industry observers note that four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.

That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

Industry observers note that four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. The Bay Area-based outfit specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion.

Fireworks co-founder Chenyu Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.

Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

It has been revealed that notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.

Fireworks, which is backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, among other firms, was assigned a $17.5 billion valuation in summer. It’s reportedly in early talks for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks mentioned it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.

Industry observers note that zhao and I spoke onstage about all of it on Thursday at Slush. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say, edited for length and clarity.

You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?

Industry observers note that when you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.

How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

Sources indicate that I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.

How far behind are open models right now?

A few years ago I’d have mentioned a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.

If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

Recent findings suggest that frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 owners and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.

In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

Recent findings suggest that we think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

Sources indicate that anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.

Recent findings suggest that fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

Every manufacturer is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.

Sources indicate that notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?

I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.

How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

Sources indicate that notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.

It has been revealed that jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?

According to recent reports, it’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron [Nvidia’s family of open AI models], and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

Breaking: NSW passes Mount Pleasant coalmine law as Greens claim change an attempt to head off One Nation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Labor notes allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’.
  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • The Upcoming South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Labor notes allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

The Upcoming South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.

At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

Recent findings suggest that “Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she noted. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”.

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT until 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

Despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation, claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas. Minns has rejected the idea the legislation goes around the high court decision.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, says this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.

“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”.

She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.

“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she said at a press conference on Thursday.

In a recent development, the Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock.

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she remarked.

The Coalition, which supported the bill, said it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the newly introduced year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell stated.

She mentioned “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

Industry observers note that the legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns said the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he noted, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

The clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent development from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW stated the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.

The Law Society of NSW stated on Thursday it was concerned that without further amendments, the Henry VIII clause risked “undermining the rule of law”.

Houssos told the upper house on Friday the government had carefully considered concerns and moved amendments to the clause because it “recognises the importance of appropriate safeguards and accountability”.

The organization has called the idea “nonsense.”.

Sources indicate that the Donald Trump-backed initiative that resulted in a US-led takeover of TikTok's American business has apparently inspired some leaders in the European Union. This week Germany and Austria proposed a similar move for the app's European operation, and now the German government indicates that it has lined up investors willing to fork over as much as €25 billion (about $27.4 billion USD) to finance such an arrangement, Politico reports.

"It's a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business," Berlin culture minister Wolfram Weimer told the outlet. "And TikTok Europe should be open to sell 75% to 80% of the shares." Investors from five countries have expressed interest in such a deal, according to Weimer.

Sources indicate that if you're thinking, "wait, I didn't know TikTok Europe was for sale," that's because... it isn't. At least not in any official sense. And unsurprisingly, it doesn't seem like ByteDance is at all interested in this arrangement, which a spokesperson has described as "nonsense." Of course, TikTok's US business wasn't officially for sale either. But we all know how that ended.

Sources indicate that whether a similar EU-led takeover of TikTok would actually gain any traction is unclear. The app isn't facing a ban in the region. And, as Bloomberg, pointed out earlier this week, Germany and Austria likely can't strongarm the tech giant into a sale without the backing of the whole European Commission.

It has been revealed that EU officials have raised similar concerns as their US counterparts about TikTok's influence and its ties to China. Last year, the EU fined the tech giant more than $600 million for breaking EU privacy laws by funneling some EU user data to China. More recently, regulators have accused the company of breaking its Digital Services Act (DSA) with its "For You" algorithm. The EU Commission has told the company to change the design of its algorithm or it risks another massive fine.

#35770. Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1290 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.
  • Wireless industry lobby group CTIA mentioned a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls.
  • The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Wireless industry lobby group CTIA mentioned a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:.

The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA noted the pilot test shows “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”.

It has been revealed that the FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr stated. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”.

The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

Carr said that “contraband cell phones continue to pour into prisons by the thousands each year,” with “estimates indicat[ing] that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices.” He said the phones have been used to strategy scams, drug trafficking, and violent attacks.

“In Georgia, an incarcerated gang leader directed a drive-by shooting that killed two 13-year-old boys at a birthday party,” Carr stated, referring to a 2024 shooting.

Carr defended the plan against criticism that it will block legitimate communications outside the prisons, saying it includes safeguards to prevent that.

“Those that want to use the technology will apply to the FCC, explain how they plan to deploy it, and show through testing that it stays inside the designated area and doesn’t interfere with lawful communications outside the prison walls,” Carr said. “Communities nearby will receive notice before operations start. We’re also seeking comment on next steps, including ways to close remaining loopholes on other frequencies and the possibility of quiet zones around correctional facilities.”.

Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern stated the FCC should have considered the benefits of contraband phones being used to document abuses inside prisons.

It has been revealed that “Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country and people wishing to expose abuses and inhumane conditions from the inside often do not have many options,” Stern wrote in a letter to FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez’s office, which was included on the FCC docket. “Last year’s Oscar-nominated film, The Alabama Solution, used footage incarcerated people captured with contraband cell phones to show Americans some of the awful things that go on in state prisons that they’d have no other way of seeing. The same footage bolstered an ongoing DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons and was crucial evidence in a civil lawsuit by Steven Davis, who was brutally killed by prison guards, that eventually settled.”.

Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by prison phone companies ViaPath (aka Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, the National District Attorneys Association, the Correctional Leaders Association, and National Association of Police Organizations.

According to recent reports, “Inmates have used these phones to coordinate attacks against correctional officers and their families, as well as inmate violence, strikes, disturbances, and full-scale riots,” the National Association of Police Organizations remarked. “They also use contraband phones to organize deliveries of illegal drugs and weapons into correctional facilities. These dangers underscore the need to authorize indoor jamming in state and local correctional facilities.”.

Gomez, the only Democrat on the three-member commission, remarked she’s concerned about potential unintended consequences, but voted with Republicans to allow jamming after safeguards were added to the order.

“For the last 90 years, the Federal Communications Commission has prohibited jamming by non-federal actors and even prohibited jamming equipment to be introduced into the American market,” Gomez said. “That is because jamming devices are specifically designed to interfere with communications devices in order to render them un-usable.”.

Gomez said that “jamming can prevent devices from completing 911 and emergency calls as well as interfere with communications networks used by fire, police, Emergency Medical Services, and other public safety entities.” She also said making jamming equipment available in the American market could lead to “unauthorized sale of this hazardous equipment,” and that “the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise.” Criminals have used “Wi-Fi jammers to disrupt security systems, security cameras, and cellphones to conduct robberies at homes and at stores,” she said.

Gomez stated she’s glad the final order includes safeguards “to ensure that jamming is contained to this unique use, to permit jamming by a very limited category of authorized actors, and to take as much care as possible to prevent jamming and jamming equipment from becoming a hazard to safety.”.

Recent findings suggest that gomez partially dissented because she is worried the FCC will let correctional facilities and prison phone companies charge higher prices for inmate calling services that connect inmates with family members. Under US law, the FCC sets limits on those prices and considers prisons’ and jails’ safety and security costs when deciding how much money they can charge, she said.

It has been revealed that gomez mentioned, “While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures… Jamming is specifically designed to block communications and is certainly not necessary to provide phone and video calls for incarcerated individuals. We should have made this clear in today’s order. Because we failed to do so, I dissent in part.”.

The FCC order could be challenged in court. The CTIA has argued that the FCC “has no authority to allow jamming” under the Communications Act, which directs the FCC to prevent interference.

It has been revealed that AT&T mentioned the FCC’s legal justification “is premised on a fundamental factual error: the assumption that jammers will only block ‘unauthorized’ communications without impacting lawful uses. There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others. That is because radio jammers ‘block all wireless communications on affected spectrum bands,’ and, as the FCC has noted in the past, ‘cannot differentiate between contraband devices and legitimate devices.’”.

Recent findings suggest that AT&T said that “there is simply no way to limit the reach of jammers to the confines of a given facility. Jammers have been shown to cause interference outside the facilities in which they operate, greatly increasing the risk that someone living or traveling nearby will be impacted.”.

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

Below you can follow the latest updates from Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, 20th November:.

According to recent reports, french President Emmanuel Macron on Friday described Russia's actions in Ukraine and Europe as an "irresponsible gamble" that would only increase European resolve. "By escalating its war of aggression against Ukraine and also pursuing an aggressive agenda on European soil, Russia is making an irresponsible gamble that can only further isolate it and strengthen the resolve and unity of Europeans, and of all those who want to work towards peace and stability on our continent," he wrote on X.

Macron posted his comments after Moscow hit Ukraine with massive strikes and two Russian missiles appeared to have landed in Poland.

Denmark meanwhile accused Russia of attempting to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper on its soil.

US President Donald Trump has defended his admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin while deflecting a reporter's question as to whether the Russian strongman is a friend to the United States or just the president.

Sources indicate that "I can't speak to America" but mentioned: "I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship [with]. It's actually very good.".

Trump said the two bonded over the 2016 US presidential election, which Democrats say involved Russian meddling on Trump's behalf, charges that Trump rejects as what he has branded the "Russia hoax.".

The US leader also noted it will be hard to end the war in Ukraine — something he said he would easily do on his first day back in office nearly two years ago — because of the animosity between Putin and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"It's a very hard thing to do, to be honest. You have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other.".

Once again, Trump also claimed, with no real world evidence, that Putin would "love to end the war" that he debuted in February 2022, despite the fact that Russia launched massive attacks on neighboring Ukraine as soon as his meeting with Trump and Xi had ended.

US President Donald Trump, fresh back from meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, told reporters on Friday during a one-and-a-half-hour press conference that he had "very good" talks with Putin on Ukraine.

Trump noted he could not speak about security guarantees for Kyiv because there was no peace deal in place to end Russia's ongoing invasion after over four and a half years.

But the US president remarked aggressor Putin — whom Trump proudly called "my friend" when the two met in this week — "clearly expressed his desire to see the war in Ukraine end by diplomatic means.".

Trump also did not detail the conditions Moscow would place on Ukraine for such a diplomatic settlement.

On Friday, Russia introduced a massive air attack against Ukraine, with two missiles also landing in Poland, a NATO member.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius "welcomed in every respect" a move by Russian President Vladimir Putin to consult Europeans on the future of Ukraine (see entries below for more details).

During a trip to the Polish capital Warsaw, Pistorius added that declining such an invitation to Moscow would send the "completely wrong signal.".

Recent findings suggest that "We need to talk. Only by talking can we ultimately achieve results," he mentioned.

Pistorius mentioned reaching an agreement was the goal — not simply sitting down in a room together.

"He [Putin] must now show that he truly means what he claims and that he will then take the necessary steps to ensure that, at the very least, a ceasefire is established and that peace-sustaining stability can once again take hold in Europe," the German minister noted.

The comments came the same day a pair of Russian missiles and a drone were reported to have violated Polish airspace (see entries below).

While Russian officials said Germany, France and the UK had been invited to send representatives to talks on Ukraine, no details about a time or place for such talks have been announced.

Denmark's PET intelligence service has remarked it suspected Russia was behind a plot to kill a US-Ukrainian rapper at a Copenhagen concert.

"In our assessment, this case reveals that Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out a targeted killing in Denmark," PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told a news conference.

Kieffer-Kristensen added that Russia was suspected of enlisting the help of a local criminal gang for the killing.

The Danish Foreign Ministry subsequently summoned the Russian ambassador and expelled the Russian Embassy's defense attache, Foreign Minister Lars ​Lokke ​Rasmussen remarked.

The foreign minister also called on European countries to stop issuing visas to Russians and mentioned the Danish government would have taken harsher steps if Russia had a larger diplomatic presence in Denmark.

This week, Ukraine rolled out a series of strikes on the Kerch bridge, which links occupied Crimea to mainland Russia.

The 19-kilometer (12-mile) bridge has both rail and roadways, part of which has been destroyed in the strikes.

The bridge is widely seen as a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, and damage to it is regarded as a significant psychological blow to Moscow.

Following the strikes, Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate and warned the response would be "far more painful" than the damage Ukraine had caused to the Kerch bridge, as seen in the sliding image below.

At least 1,144 children were killed or injured in Ukraine during the first 10 months of 2026, the United Nations said.

UNICEF, the UN's children's agency, stated that between January and October, at least 114 children were killed and 1,030 injured.

The agency said it was the highest number of casualties seen in more than 3 years.

"That is more than three children who have been killed or injured every single day" this year, stated UNICEF spokeswoman Louise Wateridge.

Last month alone, at least 146 children were killed or injured across Ukraine, the UN agency stated.

"Attacks involving missiles and armed drones continue to put children and families at risk in their homes, schools, and communities, including far from the frontline," UNICEF warned.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Russia's violation of Polish airspace "utterly unacceptable.".

According to recent reports, "The incursion into ​Polish airspace is utterly unacceptable. I condemn it unreservedly," ​Burnham said at an EU-UK ​summit press conference ‌in Brussels.

The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the "Coalition of the Willing" that ​groups allies of Ukraine, including the UK.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting remarked the move was a Russian provocation aimed at dividing Europe.

It has been revealed that "Europe ​will not be ‌deterred from our support for Ukraine," Streeting noted. "We will not allow ⁠Putin to divide our continent, and we recognise that the ⁠frontline ​in Ukraine is the frontline for freedom and democracy everywhere.".

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov has reportedly invited representatives from Germany, France and the UK to Moscow for talks on the war in Ukraine, according to Russian news agency Interfax.

"We are waiting for a reply," the diplomat was reported to have remarked.

On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said European officials would be invited to Moscow to discuss whether they should participate in US-led talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

Interfax reported that Ryabkov stressed that such a visit would not automatically mean that European nations would be involved in the negotiations on ending the war on Ukraine.

A statement from the French president's office noted Europeans were ready to visit Moscow if given a full role in Ukraine talks.

"Our requirement will be that the opening or formalisation of this dialogue clearly signify, from the Russian perspective, that Europeans have their full role in the negotiations and participate actively in the next round of talks with the United States and Ukraine," an advisor to President Emmanuel Macron told reporters. European leaders have been pushing for a seat at the negotiation table, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying on Thursday that the outcome of the war in Ukraine would determine European security for years to come.

The European Commission said it has released another €7.9 billion ($8.67 billion) ‌to ⁠Ukraine to support the country's finances and keep public administration running.

According to recent reports, "Ukraine continues to deliver on reforms, while defending itself each and every day. Today, we are disbursing nearly €8 billion — this is the largest payment made so far," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

In a recent development, "This makes it clear: real progress on reforms brings real results and benefits. As Ukraine perseveres and moves further on its European path, they can count on our support," said von der Leyen.

It’s the ninth disbursement of funds under the mechanism to support Ukraine.

With today's release of funds, the EU and its member states have provided €245.5 billion in overall support to Ukraine, which includes €3.8 billion from the proceeds of immobilized Russian assets.

The German Foreign Ministry has expressed its support for Poland after reports a Russian missile had entered Polish airspace.

It has been revealed that "Russian missiles have once again violated Polish airspace. This is part of Russia's ongoing provocations," Germany's Foreign Ministry said in a statement on X.

"Instead of signaling a willingness to negotiate, Putin is signaling the opposite: he is opting for confrontation," the post remarked.

"We stand firmly by our neighbor and NATO ally Poland," the statement concluded.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte mentioned he had spoken to Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk about what he called "grave violations of Polish airspace overnight.".

Rutte remarked that NATO jets had been scrambled in response.

"We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend," Rutte stated.

"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine," the NATO chief said.

Recent findings suggest that "I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine," Rutte said.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot mentioned that Paris had requested a UN Security Council meeting after Russia debuted one of the war's largest missile attacks on Ukraine.

"The Kremlin has struck Kyiv again. Civilians have been killed," Jean-Noel Barrot stated on X.

It has been revealed that "These are crimes. France condemns them in the strongest possible terms," Barrot said.

Recent findings suggest that "I have requested a meeting of the United Nations Security Council. Russia will have to answer for its actions there," said France's top diplomat.

On Thursday at the Coalition of the Willing talks in Berlin, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Ukraine needed to be able to defend itself and that allies needed to ensure Kyiv had the means to do so.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, anthropic became a public tech giant on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The tech giant noted that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The manufacturer points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”.

With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously confirmed $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

It has been revealed that 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the firm. Amazon also now has a massive stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab claims.

More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

According to recent reports, anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

Recent findings suggest that all told, the manufacturer has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The historic launch is happening while Rockstar workers vote on union recognition.

Unsurprisingly, a lot of people have bought Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar Games unveiled Friday that, based on organization estimates, the open-world crime game made $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales and sold 32.5 million copies in pre-release. That last total is notably above the 20 million pre-orders some analysts expected Rockstar to sell ahead of the game's launch.

"It is with immense gratitude that we enter a upcoming chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI," Sam Houser, Rockstar's president and founder, stated in a statement. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you.".

GTA 6 has easily lapped the previous entry in the series, Grand Theft Auto 5, which made over $800 million worldwide from about 11 million units in its first day of sales in 2013. GTA 6 is more expensive, starting at $80 rather than GTA V's $60, but clearly demand has built up in the 13 years it took Rockstar to get the series' latest entry ready for launch.

It has been revealed that after years of industry-wide layoffs, it's not clear if the game's early success will actually translate into security for Rockstar Games' workers. According to a Guardian op-ed from a Rockstar North developer, the studio's staff are worried that layoffs could happen even though the game is making money hand over fist. Rockstar workers are voting on whether they'll recognize their branch of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain between November 12 and November 26. "We go where the team goes," Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar's head of publishing, told Bloomberg in October. "So if they want a union, they will have a union.".

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, Rockstar has been accused of union busting. The studio laid off a group of more than 30 developers in October 2025, most of whom were trying to organize its workers. Rockstar claims it terminated its former employees because they were sharing confidential information, and their case has played out in an employment tribunal in the lead-up to GTA 6's release. The result of the union vote or the tribunal could shape the studio's future just as much as its latest game being a smash hit.
